blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how high-level code translates into instructions a computer can execute? Welcome to the world of assembly language, where we explore the building blocks of computer operations.

blocks.markdown: Assembly language serves as a bridge between high-level programming languages and machine code. It provides a human-readable format for the instructions that a processor executes. In this lesson, we will explore the basics of assembly language, focusing on registers, load/store operations, arithmetic instructions, and branching.

blocks.title: Registers
blocks.text: Registers are small, fast storage locations within the CPU used to hold data temporarily during instruction execution. They are crucial for performing operations efficiently.

blocks.markdown: In assembly language, operations are performed on data stored in registers. Let's consider a simple arithmetic operation: adding two numbers. In a high-level language, you might write `c = a + b;`. In assembly, this operation involves loading values into registers, performing the addition, and storing the result.

blocks.caption: This instruction adds the contents of registers R2 and R3 and stores the result in R1.

blocks.title: Translating Arithmetic to Assembly
blocks.prompt: Translate the arithmetic expression `c = a + b` into assembly instructions.

steps.text: Assume `a` is stored in memory location 1000 and `b` in location 1004. First, load these values into registers.
Add the values in R2 and R3, storing the result in R1: `ADD R1, R2, R3`.
Store the result from R1 back into memory location 1008 for `c`: `STORE 1008, R1`.

blocks.answer: LOAD R2, 1000; LOAD R3, 1004; ADD R1, R2, R3; STORE 1008, R1

blocks.title: Load/Store Discipline
blocks.text: In assembly language, data must be loaded from memory into registers before it can be manipulated. After processing, results are stored back into memory.

blocks.markdown: Branching is another fundamental concept in assembly language. It allows the program to make decisions and change the flow of execution based on conditions. A common instruction for this is `BEQ` (Branch if Equal), which alters the program counter if two registers contain equal values.

blocks.title: Using Branch Instructions
blocks.prompt: Write an assembly snippet that compares two numbers and branches to a label `EQUAL` if they are equal.

steps.text: Assume the numbers are in registers R4 and R5.
Use the `SUB` instruction to compare: `SUB R6, R4, R5`.

blocks.answer: SUB R6, R4, R5; BEQ R6, 0, EQUAL

rows: Load data from memory M into register R
Store data from register R into memory M
Add contents of R2 and R3, store in R1
Subtract contents of R3 from R2, store in R1
Branch to label L if R equals 0
blocks.caption: Common Assembly Instructions

points: Registers are used for temporary data storage during processing.
Assembly language requires explicit load/store operations for memory access.
Branch instructions control the flow of execution based on conditions.
